patient.name: Maria Alvarez
patient.chief_complaint: fever and new confusion since yesterday, not eating or drinking

findings.detail: High-risk age group: geriatric (age 78) with a concurrent abnormal finding — blunted physiologic response can mask severity

physician_summary.urgency_statement: Immediate physician evaluation required: 78-year-old with sepsis physiology, hypoxia, and altered mental status.
physician_summary.clinical_concerns: Elderly patient presenting with fever, new confusion, and poor oral intake now manifesting tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, and borderline hypotension — a pattern highly concerning for sepsis, likely with a respiratory or urinary source, superimposed on possible dehydration and delirium. The combination of hypoxia and altered mental status raises risk for rapid decompensation, and age increases risk of atypical presentation and poor physiologic reserve. Differential includes severe pneumonia/sepsis, urosepsis, or other systemic infection with early septic shock.
recommended_actions: Initiate sepsis protocol: obtain blood cultures x2, lactate, CBC, CMP, procalcitonin before antibiotics
Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour per sepsis bundle
Administer supplemental oxygen to target SpO2 >92%; prepare for possible escalation of respiratory support
Initiate IV fluid resuscitation (consider 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, reassess for fluid tolerance given age)
Obtain portable chest X-ray and urinalysis/urine culture to identify infection source
Continuous cardiac and pulse oximetry monitoring; repeat vitals every 15 minutes
Assess mental status (rule out delirium vs. hypoxia-driven encephalopathy); consider CT head if no rapid improvement
Establish second large-bore IV access and consider central line/vasopressor readiness if hypotension progresses
Notify ICU/rapid response team for potential escalation of care

triage_result.esi_rationale: ESI 2 — high-risk presentation that cannot wait. The complaint describes new confusion (altered mental status) with fever in a 78-year-old, which ESI v4 lists explicitly as an ESI 2 presentation (suspected sepsis, new confusion or lethargy in the elderly). Vital signs reinforce rather than soften this: HR 134, RR 32, SpO2 89%, temp 39.4°C, and SBP 96 mmHg together meet qSOFA/SIRS criteria for sepsis with impending shock. The patient is not currently ESI 1 because there is no immediate life-saving intervention in progress — airway is intact, the patient is confused but responsive, and hypoxia is expected to correct with supplemental oxygen rather than assisted ventilation. Immediate escalation to ESI 1 is warranted if mental status declines further, SpO2 fails to rise above 92% on supplemental oxygen, or SBP falls below 90 mmHg despite fluids.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning: 78-year-old geriatric patient presenting with fever, new-onset confusion since yesterday, and poor oral intake — a classic sepsis presentation in the elderly, in whom altered mental status is often the only early localizing sign. Objective data support systemic infection with organ dysfunction: temperature 39.4°C, marked tachycardia at 134 bpm, severe tachypnea at 32 breaths/min, hypoxia at 89% on room air, and borderline hypotension at 96/58 mmHg. qSOFA is positive on at least two counts (RR ≥22, altered mentation) with borderline SBP, placing this patient at high risk for progression to septic shock. The hypoxia and tachypnea raise concern for pneumonia as the source, though urinary tract infection is equally common in this age group and reduced intake suggests significant volume depletion contributing to the hypotension and tachycardia. Decreased oral intake over 24+ hours in a 61 kg elderly patient also risks acute kidney injury and electrolyte derangement. This work-up will consume far more than two resources (labs, cultures, lactate, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, chest imaging, likely admission), but resource counting is not the governing decision point here — the patient meets ESI 2 on high-risk criteria alone and must be moved to a treatment area ahead of all lower-acuity patients. Time-to-antibiotics is the key outcome driver.
recommended_interventions: Move immediately to a monitored treatment bed — do not leave in the waiting room; notify the emergency physician and activate the sepsis/code sepsis protocol now
Apply supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula or non-rebreather, titrating to SpO2 ≥92%; escalate airway support if work of breathing worsens or saturation fails to improve
Establish two large-bore IV lines and begin balanced crystalloid resuscitation (approximately 30 mL/kg ≈ 1830 mL for 61 kg) per sepsis protocol, with close reassessment for fluid tolerance given age
Draw blood cultures x2 from separate sites BEFORE antibiotics, plus serum lactate, CBC with differential, CMP, and coagulation studies
Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition, after cultures are obtained — do not delay for imaging results
Obtain portable chest X-ray, urinalysis with culture (straight catheter specimen if unable to void), and 12-lead ECG given tachycardia
Place on continuous cardiac, pulse oximetry, and blood pressure monitoring with vital signs every 15 minutes until stabilized
Perform and document baseline neurological assessment and GCS; obtain point-of-care glucose to rule out hypoglycemia as a contributor to confusion
Initiate strict intake/output monitoring; consider indwelling catheter if hemodynamically unstable and hourly urine output tracking is required
Institute fall and delirium precautions — bed low, side rails up, frequent reorientation, call bell within reach
Contact family or caregiver for baseline mental status, medication list, advance directives, and code status clarification

patient.name: Daniel Okafor
patient.chief_complaint: crushing chest pain radiating to jaw and left arm, diaphoretic, started 40 minutes ago

physician_summary.urgency_statement: IMMEDIATE ATTENTION REQUIRED: ESI-1 patient with suspected acute coronary syndrome and hemodynamic compromise.
physician_summary.clinical_concerns: 62-year-old presenting with crushing chest pain radiating to jaw and left arm, diaphoresis, onset 40 minutes ago — classic presentation for acute myocardial infarction. Concurrent hypotension (88/54) and tachycardia (112 bpm) raise concern for cardiogenic shock or evolving hemodynamic instability. Borderline hypoxemia (SpO2 93%) may reflect pulmonary congestion from cardiac dysfunction. This constellation requires immediate cardiac workup and hemodynamic stabilization to prevent deterioration or cardiac arrest.
recommended_actions: Obtain STAT 12-lead ECG and activate cardiac catheterization lab if STEMI confirmed
Draw STAT troponin, CBC, BMP, coagulation panel, and type & screen
Establish two large-bore IVs and begin cautious IV fluid bolus given hypotension
Apply supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥94%
Administer aspirin 325 mg chewed if no contraindication; hold nitrates given hypotension
Continuous cardiac and BP monitoring; prepare for possible vasopressor support
Consult cardiology immediately for emergent evaluation
Reassess for signs of cardiogenic shock (mental status, urine output, skin perfusion)

triage_result.esi_rationale: ESI 1 — the patient requires immediate life-saving intervention. Crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm plus diaphoresis, onset 40 minutes ago, is a high-probability acute coronary syndrome, and it is accompanied by critical hypotension (SBP 88 mmHg, below the <90 critical threshold) with compensatory tachycardia (HR 112) and borderline oxygenation (SpO2 93%). Hemodynamic instability in the setting of an evolving infarct represents cardiogenic shock physiology requiring immediate stabilization — IV access and fluid/vasopressor decision-making, continuous monitoring, and emergent cath lab activation — not merely 'should not wait' (ESI 2) placement. Decision Point A is satisfied, so the algorithm stops before resource counting or the Decision Point D upgrade pathway.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning: 62-year-old male, 94 kg, with a 40-minute history of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm with diaphoresis — a classic high-risk ACS presentation well inside the reperfusion window. The distinguishing feature is hemodynamic compromise: SBP 88/54 mmHg with HR 112 and SpO2 93%. In an acute MI this pattern suggests either significant left ventricular dysfunction with early cardiogenic shock or an inferior/right-ventricular infarct with preload dependence — a critical distinction, since nitrates would be harmful in the latter and in any hypotensive ACS patient. Narrow pulse pressure (34 mmHg) and diaphoresis support poor forward flow rather than a spurious reading. Time-critical: myocardial salvage is measured in minutes, and shock physiology dramatically raises mortality. The patient must bypass triage and go directly to a resuscitation bay. Anticipated needs include 12-lead ECG within minutes, dual large-bore IV access, cardiac biomarkers and full labs, portable chest imaging, bedside echo to assess RV involvement and effusion, cautious fluid challenge, and STEMI/cath lab activation. Airway is currently intact and mentation is not described as altered, but both require continuous reassessment given the borderline SpO2 and hypotension.
recommended_interventions: Move immediately to a resuscitation bay — do not place in the waiting area; notify attending physician and activate STEMI/cardiac alert team
Obtain a 12-lead ECG within 5 minutes of arrival and have the physician interpret it at the bedside; repeat serially if initial ECG is non-diagnostic
Place patient on continuous cardiac monitoring, continuous pulse oximetry, and automated BP cycling every 5 minutes; apply defibrillator pads given arrhythmia and arrest risk
Establish two large-bore IVs (18 G or larger) and draw troponin, CBC, CMP/electrolytes, coagulation studies, and type and screen
Recheck blood pressure manually in both arms and confirm hypotension; assess for pulse-pressure narrowing and signs of poor perfusion (skin, capillary refill, mentation)
Withhold nitroglycerin and other preload-reducing agents while SBP is 88 mmHg — flag the hypotension to the physician before any vasodilator is given
Administer supplemental oxygen titrated to SpO2 ≥94%, starting with 2–4 L/min nasal cannula, and reassess response

Anticipate and prepare a cautious IV crystalloid bolus (250–500 mL) per physician order for possible RV infarct, with reassessment for pulmonary congestion after each bolus; have vasopressors available
Prepare aspirin 324 mg chewable per physician order if no contraindication; confirm antiplatelet/anticoagulant history and allergies
Obtain bedside echocardiogram and portable chest radiograph to evaluate RV function, wall motion, effusion, and pulmonary edema
Keep patient NPO, maintain strict bed rest, and place on a cardiac-arrest-ready setup; ensure airway and suction equipment are immediately at hand
Document precise symptom onset time (40 minutes prior to arrival) for reperfusion timing and reassess pain score and vital signs every 5 minutes

patient.name: Grace Lindqvist
patient.chief_complaint: sudden severe headache while lifting, worst of my life, photophobia

physician_summary.urgency_statement: Immediate physician evaluation required — thunderclap headache with red-flag features, concerning for subarachnoid hemorrhage.
trigger_reasons: Chief complaint of sudden-onset, worst-of-life headache with exertional trigger and photophobia — high-risk history for SAH
abnormal_vitals: BP 168/96 mmHg — elevated, hypertensive urgency range
physician_summary.clinical_concerns: 34-year-old presenting with sudden, severe headache described as the worst of their life, triggered by lifting and accompanied by photophobia. This symptom pattern is a classic red flag for subarachnoid hemorrhage or other acute intracranial pathology despite otherwise reassuring vitals aside from mild hypertension. Absence of fever and normal SpO2/HR/RR do not rule out serious intracranial cause. Rapid evaluation is critical given the narrow therapeutic window for diagnosis and intervention in SAH.
recommended_actions: Obtain immediate non-contrast CT head; if negative and clinical suspicion remains, proceed to CT angiography or lumbar puncture to assess for xanthochromia
Establish IV access and continuous cardiac/BP monitoring
Control BP cautiously if needed per neuro-protective protocol, avoiding precipitous drops
Perform focused neurologic exam including pupillary response, Glasgow Coma Scale, and signs of meningismus
Administer analgesia and antiemetics as needed while maintaining neuro exam validity
Consult neurology/neurosurgery early if imaging reveals hemorrhage or aneurysm
Reassess vitals and neuro status frequently pending imaging results

triage_result.esi_rationale: ESI 2 by Decision Point B: this is a high-risk situation. Sudden-onset, maximal-intensity ("worst of my life") headache with exertional onset and photophobia is a classic thunderclap presentation concerning for subarachnoid hemorrhage — a time-dependent, potentially catastrophic diagnosis. The patient is also in severe pain. Although all vital signs are within threshold ranges and the patient currently appears stable, ESI 2 is driven by trajectory and worst-case risk, not present appearance. This patient should not wait in the waiting room.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning:
34-year-old presenting with abrupt, severe headache that began during lifting (Valsalva/exertional trigger), described as the worst of his/her life, accompanied by photophobia. This constellation is the textbook thunderclap headache and must be assumed to be aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise; differential also includes cervical or vertebral artery dissection, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, and pituitary apoplexy. Photophobia suggests meningeal irritation, consistent with subarachnoid blood.

Vital signs are reassuring on the surface — HR 98, RR 16, SpO2 98%, temp 36.8°C — and none cross concerning thresholds. BP 168/96 is below the 180/110 concerning cut-offs but is elevated for a 34-year-old and may reflect pain, sympathetic surge, or a Cushing-type response to rising intracranial pressure; it warrants serial monitoring rather than dismissal. Normal vitals do not lower the acuity here: a substantial proportion of SAH patients are hemodynamically normal at first contact and deteriorate abruptly with rebleeding, which carries very high mortality.

No altered mental status, focal deficit, seizure, or syncope is reported, so ESI 1 criteria (need for immediate life-saving intervention) are not met at this time. However, the resource count is irrelevant to the assignment — Decision Point B stops the algorithm at ESI 2 before resource prediction. The anticipated work-up (non-contrast head CT emergently, possible lumbar puncture or CTA, IV access, labs, analgesia, neurosurgical consult) would independently exceed two resources.

Key risk: neurologic deterioration can be sudden. This patient requires continuous observation in a monitored treatment space, not a waiting area.
recommended_interventions: Place immediately in a monitored treatment bed — do not return to waiting room; notify the emergency physician now
Expedite non-contrast head CT as the highest priority; flag as possible subarachnoid hemorrhage so imaging is not delayed
Establish two large-bore IV lines and draw CBC, chemistry, coagulation studies, and type and screen
Apply continuous cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, and automated BP cycling every 5–15 minutes

Perform and document a baseline neurologic assessment (GCS, pupils, cranial nerves, limb strength) and repeat at least every 15 minutes; escalate immediately for any decline in GCS, new focal deficit, vomiting, or seizure
Keep head of bed elevated to approximately 30 degrees and maintain a quiet, dimly lit environment for photophobia
Give analgesia per protocol with the physician — avoid antiplatelet agents such as aspirin or NSAIDs until hemorrhage is excluded; add an antiemetic for nausea/vomiting
Keep patient NPO pending imaging and possible lumbar puncture or procedural intervention
Report the elevated BP (168/96) to the physician and clarify treatment parameters, as aggressive lowering may be desired to reduce rebleeding risk once SAH is suspected
Anticipate and pre-alert neurosurgery/neurology consultation and prepare for possible lumbar puncture if CT is non-diagnostic

patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.chief_complaint: prior episode of syncope last year, today has chest pressure with exertion

physician_summary.urgency_statement: ESI-2 patient with hypertensive urgency and exertional chest pressure — requires immediate physician evaluation.
trigger_reasons: ESI acuity level 2 meets immediate-attention threshold
Severe hypertension with systolic BP 186 mmHg
Exertional chest pressure with history of syncope
physician_summary.clinical_concerns: 58-year-old presenting with exertional chest pressure and a history of syncope within the past year, now found to have severely elevated blood pressure (186/104 mmHg) meeting criteria for hypertensive urgency. The combination of chest pressure with exertion and prior syncope raises concern for underlying coronary artery disease, unstable angina, or a cardiac arrhythmic process contributing to both the syncopal event and current symptoms. Hypertensive urgency itself increases myocardial oxygen demand and may be precipitating or exacerbating the chest pressure. Immediate cardiac risk stratification is warranted given the potential for acute coronary syndrome or a cardiogenic cause of the prior syncope.
recommended_actions: Obtain 12-lead ECG immediately to assess for ischemia, arrhythmia, or conduction abnormality
Initiate continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry
Draw troponin and repeat in serial fashion per ACS protocol
Establish IV access and send basic metabolic panel, CBC, and BNP
Administer antihypertensive therapy per protocol to gradually reduce BP while avoiding precipitous drops
Perform focused cardiac and pulmonary exam; assess for signs of heart failure or aortic pathology
Consider portable chest X-ray to evaluate for pulmonary edema or mediastinal widening
Obtain detailed history of syncope episode including triggers, prodrome, and associated symptoms
Consult cardiology given chest pressure with exertion, syncope history, and hypertensive urgency
Reassess vitals frequently and escalate care if BP remains uncontrolled or symptoms worsen

triage_result.esi_rationale: ESI 2 — high-risk presentation. A 58-year-old with exertional chest pressure is a classic anginal/acute coronary syndrome presentation until proven otherwise, and the clinical situation carries a credible threat to life or organ function if evaluation is delayed. He is not currently in extremis requiring an immediate life-saving intervention (Decision Point A negative — airway patent, SpO2 98%, HR 88, perfusing pressure), so ESI 1 does not apply. Decision Point B is answered yes on the high-risk criterion, so the algorithm stops before resource counting. Reinforcing this, the work-up would consume well more than two resources (ECG plus serial troponins, labs, IV access, cardiac monitoring, possible imaging and cardiology consult), and the measured hypertensive urgency (SBP 186, DBP 104) is an out-of-range vital sign that per Decision Point D supports upgrading rather than holding at ESI 3. This patient should not wait in the lobby.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning: 58-year-old male, 70 kg, presenting with chest pressure provoked by exertion. The exertional character is the key discriminator: symptoms reproduced by increased myocardial oxygen demand and the substernal 'pressure' quality are the textbook description of angina, and in a 58-year-old this places acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina at the top of the differential. The documented prior syncopal episode last year is a historical finding, not part of today's presentation, but it is not clinically irrelevant — syncope in combination with exertional chest symptoms raises the possibility of a structural or outflow-obstruction cause such as severe aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, as well as an arrhythmic aetiology, and should be flagged for the treating clinician rather than dismissed. Vital signs are notable for a blood pressure of 186/104 mmHg, meeting the concerning threshold for systolic hypertension with a diastolic also above the normal range. Elevated afterload increases myocardial oxygen demand and may be both a contributor to and a consequence of ongoing ischaemia; it also has implications for anticoagulation and thrombolytic safety should ACS be confirmed. The remaining vitals are reassuring — HR 88 without tachycardia, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8°C — indicating he is currently compensated and not in cardiogenic shock or respiratory failure. That stability, however, is expected in early ACS and must not be mistaken for low acuity; an occlusive coronary lesion can decompensate abruptly into arrhythmia or arrest. Aortic dissection also warrants consideration given the markedly elevated pressure, and bilateral blood pressures should be obtained. The clinical imperative is immediate ECG acquisition to identify ST-elevation, continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia, and rapid physician evaluation. This patient requires a monitored bed now, not a waiting-room seat.
recommended_interventions: Obtain 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival and hand directly to the emergency physician for immediate interpretation; repeat if symptoms change or recur
Place patient in a monitored treatment bed — do not return to waiting room
Initiate continuous cardiac telemetry, pulse oximetry, and automated BP cycling every 5–15 minutes
Establish IV access with two large-bore cannulae and draw baseline labs including high-sensitivity troponin, CBC, electrolytes, renal function, and coagulation studies; plan serial troponin
Administer aspirin 324 mg chewable per chest pain protocol unless contraindicated (allergy, active bleeding) — confirm with physician
Assess and document pain using a 0–10 scale plus character, radiation, provoking and relieving factors, and time of onset; reassess after any intervention
Withhold supplemental oxygen while SpO2 remains ≥94% on room air; titrate only if desaturation occurs
Measure blood pressure in both arms and check bilateral radial pulses to screen for aortic dissection before any antiplatelet or anticoagulant escalation
Notify the emergency physician immediately of exertional chest pressure with hypertensive urgency and prior syncope; escalate for possible cardiology consultation
Obtain focused history on the prior syncopal episode — exertional versus positional, prodrome, witnessed duration — and auscultate for murmurs suggestive of aortic stenosis or HCM
Keep patient at rest on bed rest with head of bed elevated; nothing by mouth pending physician evaluation
Ensure defibrillator and resuscitation equipment are immediately available at the bedside
Reassess vital signs and symptom status at minimum every 15 minutes and escalate immediately for recurrent pain, dysrhythmia, hypotension, or altered mental status

patient.name: Tom Becker
patient.chief_complaint: mild abdominal pain for 3 days, eating and drinking normally, no vomiting

triage_result.esi_rationale: Not ESI 1 (no immediate life-saving intervention needed), not ESI 2 (no high-risk features, alert and oriented, pain described as mild, no severe distress). At Decision Point C, this well-appearing 35-year-old with 3 days of mild abdominal pain, normal oral intake, no vomiting, and entirely normal vital signs is anticipated to need approximately one resource — basic laboratory work (e.g., CBC/CMP, urinalysis) — making ESI 4 the most accurate assignment. Decision Point D does not apply as all vital signs are within range.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning: 35-year-old, 81 kg, presenting with 3 days of mild, non-progressive abdominal pain. Reassuring history: tolerating food and fluids normally and no vomiting, which argues against obstruction, significant gastroenteritis, or a surgical abdomen with peritoneal irritation. All measured vital signs are normal (HR 76, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 98%, T 36.8°C) — no tachycardia, no hypotension, no fever to suggest sepsis or intra-abdominal infection. No critical or concerning vocabulary symptoms were reported; the pain is explicitly characterized as mild rather than severe, and there is no vomiting, so no ESI 2 upgrade criteria are met. The subacute 3-day course with preserved intake in a hemodynamically normal patient predicts a limited work-up: screening labs with or without urinalysis, and likely no imaging or IV therapy. If the abdominal exam at bedside reveals focal peritoneal signs, a rising pain score, or if pregnancy is a consideration requiring additional testing and imaging, the resource count would rise and the patient should be re-triaged to ESI 3.
recommended_interventions: Obtain focused abdominal assessment including palpation for localized tenderness, guarding, rebound, and bowel sounds; document pain location, character, and 0-10 score
Collect urine specimen for urinalysis; obtain urine or serum pregnancy test if patient is of childbearing potential
Draw baseline labs per provider order (CBC, CMP, lipase) using a single venipuncture to limit resource use
Keep patient NPO except sips pending provider evaluation in case imaging or surgical consult becomes necessary
Offer oral analgesia per protocol for mild pain and reassess pain score within 30-60 minutes
Reassess vital signs at least every 2 hours in the waiting area and re-triage immediately if pain escalates, fever develops, vomiting begins, or tachycardia/hypotension appear
Instruct patient to notify triage nurse promptly of any worsening pain, inability to keep fluids down, or new vomiting

patient.name: Sam Whitfield
patient.chief_complaint: laceration to left forearm from kitchen knife, bleeding controlled with pressure

triage_result.esi_rationale: Patient is hemodynamically stable with all vital signs within normal range and requires exactly one anticipated resource — laceration repair (wound closure with sutures/staples/adhesive). Per ESI Decision Point C, a single anticipated resource yields ESI 4. Simple laceration requiring repair is an explicit ESI 4 exemplar. No life-saving intervention needed (Decision Point A negative), no high-risk features, altered mentation, or severe pain/distress to meet ESI 2 criteria, and Decision Point D does not apply because no vital signs are out of range.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning: 44-year-old adult presenting with an isolated traumatic laceration to the left forearm sustained from a kitchen knife. Bleeding is reported as controlled with direct pressure, indicating no ongoing hemorrhage and no need for emergent hemostatic or resuscitative measures. Vital signs are entirely reassuring — HR 92, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8°C — with no evidence of hypovolemia, shock, or compensatory tachycardia, supporting the account of controlled blood loss. The chief complaint contains no critical or concerning vocabulary symptoms; the bleeding described is explicitly controlled and localized rather than severe. Anticipated ED course is wound exploration, irrigation, and simple closure, which counts as a single resource; local anesthetic, wound cleansing, dressing, and tetanus prophylaxis are not counted as separate ESI resources. Attention should be paid at bedside to depth of injury, given the forearm's flexor tendon, neurovascular, and volar structure proximity — if examination reveals tendon involvement, arterial injury, retained foreign body requiring imaging, or need for specialty (hand surgery) consultation, the resource count would rise to two or more and the patient should be re-triaged to ESI 3.
recommended_interventions: Maintain direct pressure and apply a clean sterile pressure dressing to the left forearm; elevate the extremity above heart level
Assess and document distal neurovascular status — radial pulse, capillary refill, sensation in median/ulnar/radial distributions, and finger flexion/extension strength — before and after dressing
Inspect wound for length, depth, contamination, retained glass or metal fragments, and visible tendon or fat; escalate to ESI 3 and notify provider if deep structure involvement is suspected
Verify tetanus immunization status and administer Td/Tdap booster per protocol if last dose was more than 5 years ago for a contaminated wound or 10 years for a clean wound
Irrigate and cleanse wound with normal saline per protocol in preparation for provider evaluation and laceration repair
Assess and document pain score; offer oral analgesia per standing order and reassess response
Obtain injury mechanism details including knife cleanliness, time since injury, handedness, occupation, and any anticoagulant use or bleeding disorder history
Reassess vital signs and dressing for bleed-through every 30-60 minutes while awaiting provider evaluation
Keep patient NPO status unnecessary; reassure and instruct patient to report numbness, tingling, increasing pain, or renewed bleeding immediately

patient.name: Nina Castellanos
patient.chief_complaint: denies chest pain, here for a medication refill and blood pressure check

triage_result.esi_rationale: ESI 5 — Non-Urgent. Patient is a 29-year-old presenting for a medication refill and blood pressure check with explicitly denied chest pain. All vital signs are within normal adult ranges (HR 76, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 98%, Temp 36.8°C). No life-saving intervention is required (not ESI 1), no high-risk features, altered mental status, or severe pain/distress are present (not ESI 2), and the anticipated work-up requires no resources beyond examination and a blood pressure measurement — vital signs and physical exam are not counted as resources under ESI v4. Per Decision Point C, zero resources yields ESI 5.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning: Chief complaint is administrative/routine: medication refill plus a blood pressure recheck. The complaint explicitly documents 'denies chest pain' — a negative finding that is clinically meaningful and must not be treated as a positive chest pain presentation. There are no measured vital sign abnormalities; the blood pressure of 124/78 mmHg is normotensive, which answers the patient's stated reason for the visit and provides no basis for upgrade under Decision Point D (which applies only to patients otherwise scored ESI 3). The patient is young, hemodynamically stable, well-perfused, and in no apparent distress. Anticipated care is a focused history, review of the current antihypertensive or other maintenance medication, confirmation of adherence and tolerance, a blood pressure reading, and issuance of a prescription — all of which fall within examination-level care. Should the history uncover new symptoms, uncontrolled readings at home, or medication side effects, the assignment should be revisited and resource needs recounted.
recommended_interventions: Document the explicit denial of chest pain in the triage note as a negative finding, distinct from a chest pain presentation
Obtain and record a repeat manual blood pressure after 5 minutes of seated rest to confirm the 124/78 mmHg reading and address the patient's stated reason for visit
Verify the specific medication requiring refill, the prescribing clinician, last fill date, remaining supply, and adherence pattern
Screen briefly for interval symptoms — chest discomfort, dyspnea, headache, visual change, palpitations, edema, dizziness — and escalate triage level if any are newly reported
Review for medication side effects, drug interactions, and any new over-the-counter or herbal agents
Confirm allergy list and current medication reconciliation in the record
Provide home blood pressure monitoring education and instruct the patient to log readings
Route to fast-track or a low-acuity treatment area; no IV access, laboratory studies, or imaging indicated at this time
Arrange or confirm primary care follow-up for ongoing prescription management to reduce reliance on the emergency department for refills
Give clear return precautions for chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, or focal neurologic symptoms prior to discharge

patient.name: Alice Nguyen
patient.chief_complaint: stubbed toe on bedframe this morning, sore but weight bearing

triage_result.esi_rationale: Patient is a well-appearing 25-year-old with entirely normal vital signs and an isolated minor extremity injury. No life-saving intervention required (not ESI 1), no high-risk features, altered mental status, or severe pain/distress (not ESI 2). At Decision Point C, the anticipated work-up consists of a single resource — plain radiograph of the toe/foot to exclude fracture. Simple wound care, buddy taping, and oral analgesia are not counted as resources under ESI v4. Exactly one resource yields ESI 4. Decision Point D does not apply as all vital signs are within normal range.
triage_result.clinical_reasoning: 25-year-old presenting after blunt trauma to the toe from striking a bedframe this morning. The patient is ambulatory and weight bearing, which is a reassuring finding that argues against significant fracture or dislocation and satisfies low-risk clinical decision criteria for extremity injury. Pain is described as soreness rather than severe. Vital signs are entirely normal (HR 76, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 98%, T 36.8\u00b0C) with no measured out-of-range findings, indicating hemodynamic stability and no systemic involvement. The chief complaint contains no vocabulary symptoms from the critical or concerning lists. The only anticipated diagnostic need is a single plain film to rule out a phalangeal fracture; any subsequent management (buddy taping, footwear advice, oral analgesia) falls outside the ESI resource definition. Patient can safely wait for care. Red flags to monitor while waiting: worsening pain out of proportion, deformity, nail bed injury or subungual hematoma, open wound, loss of sensation, or inability to bear weight on re-evaluation.
recommended_interventions: Perform focused musculoskeletal exam of the affected toe and foot: inspect for deformity, rotational malalignment, open wounds, nail bed injury, and subungual hematoma
Assess and document neurovascular status distal to the injury \u2014 capillary refill, sensation, and pedal pulses
Obtain and document a pain score; offer oral analgesia (acetaminophen or NSAID) per standing order if no contraindication
Apply ice pack intermittently (20 minutes on/off) with a barrier to protect skin, and elevate the foot while waiting
Anticipate and facilitate plain radiograph of the toe/foot to exclude phalangeal fracture
Confirm tetanus immunization status, particularly if any skin breach is identified
Provide buddy taping and rigid-soled or open-toe footwear guidance per provider order after imaging
Instruct patient to notify triage staff immediately if pain escalates significantly, the toe becomes numb or discolored, or they can no longer bear weight
